paragraphs.simple: Soccer brings people from all over the world together. People watch the World Cup, and people everywhere play soccer just for fun.

background.note: The biggest soccer competition. Teams from many countries play every four years.

paragraphs.context: Since soccer often brings people together, it should be no surprise that
paragraphs.simple: While writing the book, the author met Pelé's daughter Kely and his grandson Malcolm. Pelé is one of the best soccer players ever. He no longer plays, and he lives in Brazil and helps soccer all over the world.

background.note: A famous soccer player from Brazil (1940-2022). He won the World Cup three times.

sentences.context: He wants them to travel through time and learn secrets of greatness from four people who are called great by the world.
sentences.simple: Merlin wants them to go to other times and learn secrets of being great from four famous great people.
sentences.main: He wants them to travel through time and learn secrets of greatness.

parts.text: He wants them to travel through time
parts.meaning: Merlin wants them to go to other times

parts.text: and learn secrets of greatness
parts.meaning: and find out secrets of being great

parts.text: from four people who are called great by the world.
parts.meaning: from four people that everyone says are great.

sentences.grammar: "Want someone to do something": "He wants them to travel and learn." "Are called great by the world" is passive: the world calls them great.

sentences.context: Whenever he and Annie breathed in the mist and made a wish, they magically had a great talent for one hour.
sentences.simple: Every time Jack and Annie breathed the magic mist and made a wish, they had a special talent for one hour.
sentences.main: They magically had a great talent for one hour.

parts.text: Whenever he and Annie breathed in the mist and made a wish,
parts.meaning: Every time Jack and Annie breathed the mist and wished,

parts.text: they magically had a great talent for one hour.
parts.meaning: they had a special talent for an hour, by magic.

sentences.grammar: "Whenever" = every time that. The "whenever" part can come first, followed by a comma.

sentences.context: Held every four years, the games are played for several weeks.
sentences.simple: The World Cup happens every four years, and the games go on for a few weeks.
sentences.main: The games are played for several weeks.

parts.text: Held every four years,
parts.job: Extra information about the games (past participle).
parts.meaning: The games happen every four years;

parts.text: the games are played for several weeks.
parts.meaning: people play the games for a few weeks.

sentences.grammar: A sentence can start with a past participle ("Held ...") that tells us more about the subject: "The games, which are held every four years, are played for several weeks."

sentences.context: In a sunken plaza below was a round concrete building covered with posters and murals.
sentences.simple: Down below, in a square that was lower than the street, there was a round concrete building with posters and wall paintings on it.
sentences.main: A round concrete building was in a sunken plaza below.

parts.text: In a sunken plaza below
parts.meaning: Down in a low square

parts.text: was a round concrete building
parts.meaning: there was a round concrete building

parts.text: covered with posters and murals.
parts.meaning: that had posters and big wall paintings all over it.

sentences.grammar: When a place phrase comes first, the verb can come before the subject: "In a plaza was a building" = "A building was in a plaza."

sentences.context: As it rumbled through the dark tunnel, the air in the car was suffocating.
sentences.simple: While the train went noisily through the dark tunnel, the air inside the train car was so hot that it was hard to breathe.
sentences.main: The air in the car was suffocating.

parts.text: As it rumbled through the dark tunnel,
parts.meaning: While the train went loudly through the dark tunnel,

parts.text: the air in the car was suffocating.
parts.meaning: it was very hard to breathe inside the train car.

sentences.grammar: "As" here means "while, at the same time". "It" means the train.

sentences.context: As soon as the train stopped, Jack and Annie followed the boy, squeezing past people to get to the door.
sentences.simple: Right when the train stopped, Jack and Annie went after the boy. They pushed past people to reach the door.
sentences.main: Jack and Annie followed the boy.

parts.text: As soon as the train stopped,
parts.meaning: The moment the train stopped,

parts.text: Jack and Annie followed the boy,
parts.meaning: Jack and Annie went after the boy,

parts.text: squeezing past people to get to the door.
parts.job: How they did it (-ing part), and why (to ...).
parts.meaning: pushing through people to reach the door.

sentences.grammar: "As soon as" = right after. The -ing part ("squeezing ...") adds another action at the same time. "To get to" tells the purpose.

sentences.context: The rows were so steep, it looked as if spectators in the highest rows might fall straight down onto the field.
sentences.simple: The rows of seats went up so sharply that it seemed people at the very top could fall down onto the field.

parts.text: The rows were so steep,
parts.meaning: The rows of seats went up very sharply,

parts.text: it looked as if spectators in the highest rows
parts.meaning: so it seemed that people in the top rows

parts.text: might fall straight down onto the field.
parts.meaning: could fall right down onto the field.

sentences.grammar: "So + adjective, (that) + result": "The rows were so steep (that) it looked ..." "As if" = in a way that makes you think.

sentences.context: They did have incredible seats—seats that would help them get close enough to Pelé to learn a secret of greatness from him.
sentences.simple: Their seats really were amazing. From those seats they could get near Pelé and learn a secret of greatness from him.

parts.text: They did have incredible seats—
parts.job: Main idea ("did have" makes it strong).
parts.meaning: Their seats really were amazing,

parts.text: seats that would help them get close enough to Pelé
parts.job: What the seats would do ("that" tells which seats).
parts.meaning: seats that would let them get near Pelé

parts.text: to learn a secret of greatness from him.
parts.job: Why they needed to be close.
parts.meaning: so they could learn a secret of being great from him.

sentences.grammar: "Did + verb" makes a statement stronger: "They did have" = they really had. "Close enough to ... to learn" = so close that they could learn.

sentences.context: Even though he was envious, Jack was still glad that Roberto had a great view of the game.
sentences.simple: Jack wished he had Roberto's seat, but he was happy that Roberto could see the game well.

parts.text: Even though he was envious,
parts.meaning: Jack wanted what Roberto had, but

parts.text: Jack was still glad
parts.meaning: he was happy anyway

parts.text: that Roberto had a great view of the game.
parts.meaning: that Roberto could see the game very well.

sentences.grammar: "Even though" shows a surprising contrast. "Still" means "anyway, in spite of that". "Glad that + sentence" tells why someone is happy.

sentences.context: Not only would he never get a good look at the World Cup players now—but how was he going to find Annie again?
sentences.simple: Jack could not see the players up close now. And there was a worse problem: how could he find Annie again?
sentences.main: How was he going to find Annie again?

parts.text: Not only would he never get a good look at the World Cup players now—
parts.meaning: He would not get to see the players well now,

parts.text: but how was he going to find Annie again?
parts.meaning: and also, how could he find Annie again?

sentences.grammar: "Not only ... but (also) ..." adds a second, often bigger, idea. After "not only" at the start, the verb comes before the subject: "not only would he ..."

sentences.context: The president of Mexico presented a giant trophy to Brazil, and Carlos Alberto, the captain of the team, lifted it high above his head.
sentences.simple: The president of Mexico gave Brazil a huge cup, and Carlos Alberto, Brazil's captain, held it up high over his head.
sentences.main: The president presented a trophy, and Carlos Alberto lifted it.

parts.text: The president of Mexico presented a giant trophy to Brazil,
parts.meaning: The president of Mexico gave Brazil a huge cup,

parts.text: and Carlos Alberto, the captain of the team,
parts.job: Second subject, with extra information between commas.
parts.meaning: and Carlos Alberto, Brazil's captain,

parts.text: lifted it high above his head.
parts.meaning: held the cup up high over his head.

sentences.grammar: "Present something to someone" = give it at a special event. "The captain of the team" between commas tells us who Carlos Alberto is.

sentences.context: Jack and Annie turned to Roberto, who was now holding a toddler, posing for the camera.
sentences.simple: Jack and Annie looked at Roberto. He was holding a small child and standing still so someone could take a picture.
sentences.main: Jack and Annie turned to Roberto.

parts.text: Jack and Annie turned to Roberto,
parts.meaning: Jack and Annie looked at Roberto,

parts.text: who was now holding a toddler,
parts.meaning: who was holding a little child,

parts.text: posing for the camera.
parts.job: What else he was doing (-ing part).
parts.meaning: and standing nicely for a photo.

sentences.grammar: ", who ..." adds information about a person. The -ing part ("posing ...") tells another thing Roberto was doing at the same time.

sentences.context: Then, even though there were plenty of seats, Jack, Annie, and Roberto squeezed into a two-seater so they could all sit together.
sentences.simple: The bus had many empty seats, but the three friends pushed into one seat for two people, so they could sit together.
sentences.main: Jack, Annie, and Roberto squeezed into a two-seater.

parts.text: Then, even though there were plenty of seats,
parts.meaning: There were lots of empty seats, but

parts.text: Jack, Annie, and Roberto squeezed into a two-seater
parts.meaning: the three of them pushed into a seat for two

parts.text: so they could all sit together.
parts.meaning: so that they could sit together.

sentences.grammar: "Even though" shows a surprising contrast. "So (that) + could" tells the purpose of an action.

sentences.context: Fifty-two times you have proven your courage and kindness under the most difficult of circumstances.
sentences.simple: Fifty-two times you have shown that you are brave and kind, even when things were very hard.
sentences.main: You have proven your courage and kindness.

parts.text: Fifty-two times
parts.job: How many times (put first for strong effect).
parts.meaning: On fifty-two trips

parts.text: you have proven your courage and kindness
parts.meaning: you have shown you are brave and kind

parts.text: under the most difficult of circumstances.
parts.meaning: even when things were very, very hard.

sentences.grammar: "Have proven" is the present perfect: it sums up all their trips until now. "The most difficult of circumstances" = the hardest situations.

sentences.context: In countless neighborhoods around the globe, people gather to play the game and simply to have a good time.
sentences.simple: In very many places all over the world, people meet to play soccer just for fun.
sentences.main: People gather to play the game.

parts.text: In countless neighborhoods around the globe,
parts.meaning: In very many places in the world,

parts.text: people gather to play the game
parts.meaning: people meet to play soccer

parts.text: and simply to have a good time.
parts.meaning: and just to have fun.

sentences.grammar: "To play" and "to have" both say why people gather. "Simply" = only, just.

a bit.example: She didn’t seem to be a bit worried.
a bit.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

a bunch of.meaning: A lot of; a group of.
a bunch of.example: Jack looked at their bill and left a bunch of pesos on the table.
a bunch of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

a couple of.example: “Go up this street to the big statue of the angel, turn left onto Florencia, and after a couple of blocks, ask somebody to direct you to Insurgentes—that’s in-sur-HEN-tes,” said the guard, sounding out the word.
a couple of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

a long story.meaning: "It's a long story" = it is too long and difficult to explain now.
a long story.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

a pair of.meaning: Two things that go together, or one thing with two parts, like pants.
a pair of.example: He changed into a pair of shorts and a T-shirt.
a pair of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

all over.example: “People have come to Mexico from all over South America and Europe to see this game.”
all over.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

all the way.example: She pointed all the way up.
all the way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

along with.example: But they were facing the field, pumping their arms in the air and shouting and cheering along with the crowd.
along with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

as if.meaning: In a way that makes it seem that...
as if.example: The rows were so steep, it looked as if spectators in the highest rows might fall straight down onto the field.
as if.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

as long as.example: I’ll keep looking as long as I have to!
as long as.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

as soon as.meaning: At the moment that; right after.
as soon as.example: As soon as the train stopped, Jack and Annie followed the boy, squeezing past people to get to the door.
as soon as.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

at once.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

back home.meaning: Home, where you live, when you are far away from it. "Bring you back home" means take you home again.
back home.example: “I’ll bet there’s a way to see it back home—on the computer, or on a DVD.”
back home.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

be about to.meaning: To be going to do something very soon.
be about to.example: The sun was about to rise, and birds had started to chirp in the warm summer dawn.
be about to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

be supposed to.meaning: 1. Should; to be expected to do something ("What are we supposed to do first?"). 2. "Is supposed to be" can also mean is meant to show ("the lady in the painting is supposed to be the city of Venice").
be supposed to.example: “A country’s embassy is supposed to help its citizens when they visit another country,” said Jack.
be supposed to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

belong to.meaning: If a thing belongs to you, it is yours.
belong to.example: Jack and Annie eventually found out that the tree house belonged to Morgan le Fay, a magical librarian from the legendary realm of Camelot.
belong to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

best of all.meaning: Better than all the other things; the best thing was...
best of all.example: “The Wand of Dianthus helped you learn four secrets of happiness,” said Merlin, “from Leonardo da Vinci, Basho the poet, the deep sea—and, best of all, from this little one you brought me from Antarctica.”
best of all.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

best seats in the house.meaning: The best places to sit in a theater or stadium.
best seats in the house.example: “Y’all have two of the best seats in the house!”
best seats in the house.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

big time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

blow it.meaning: To lose a good chance by making a mistake. (Friendly talk.)
blow it.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

break in.meaning: To start talking while another person is talking; to interrupt.
break in.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

break the silence.meaning: To be the first to speak after a quiet time.
break the silence.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

bring together.meaning: To make people meet or join each other.
bring together.example: Once I started researching the subject of soccer, I quickly learned that one of its most important gifts is that it brings people together from all over the world—not only as viewers of the World Cup matches, but as players, too.
bring together.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

by the time.meaning: "By the time they reached the tree" means at the moment when they reached it (and not before).
by the time.example: By the time the tram arrived at the station near the stadium, the clouds had disappeared.
by the time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

catch up to.meaning: To reach someone who is ahead of you.
catch up to.example: “We’ll catch up to them outside the stadium,” said Roberto, running alongside Jack and Annie.
catch up to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

cell phone.meaning: A mobile phone. (In 1970, there were none.)
cell phone.example: Jack wished he had a cell phone, but he knew cell phones hadn’t been invented yet.
cell phone.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

change into.meaning: To take off your clothes and put on other clothes ("He changed into shorts").
change into.example: He changed into a pair of shorts and a T-shirt.
change into.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

check out.meaning: To borrow a book from a library. (It can also mean "go and look at something".)
check out.example: Check out some exciting ones, with big adventures and interesting information.”
check out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

come back.example: But when you didn’t come back, we figured your seat must have been okay!
come back.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

come on.meaning: "Come on!" means "Hurry!", "Let's go!" or "Please do it!"
come on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

come to a stop.example: As the woman nodded, the metro train came to a stop.
come to a stop.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

deep in thought.meaning: Thinking very hard about something, so you do not notice other things.
deep in thought.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

do the right thing.meaning: To do what is good and fair.
do the right thing.example: And then, for the second time that day, he chose to do the right thing: “Yeah, sure.
do the right thing.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

draw close.example: When Jack, Annie, and Roberto drew closer, they saw about twenty boys and girls of all ages running around barefoot and covered with mud.
draw close.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

each other.meaning: Used to say that each one does something to the other one.
each other.example: How did people ever find each other in 1970?
each other.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

even if.meaning: It does not matter if this happens; the result is the same.
even if.example: Not even if we didn’t have a mission and were the best players in the world,” said Jack.
even if.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

excuse me.meaning: A polite way to start talking to someone you do not know, or to say sorry.
excuse me.example: “Excuse me,” Jack interrupted, “but do you know when the match starts?
excuse me.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

extra time.meaning: In soccer, more time added at the end of a game when the score is equal.
extra time.example: “Italy scored five goals in extra time!”
extra time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

fall asleep.example: They’d all fallen asleep on the long ride back to the city.
fall asleep.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

far out.meaning: "Far out!" = great! wonderful! (Slang from the 1960s and 1970s.)
far out.usageNote: You only need to understand it for this story.

faster and faster.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

find out.meaning: To learn a fact that you did not know.
find out.example: Jack and Annie eventually found out that the tree house belonged to Morgan le Fay, a magical librarian from the legendary realm of Camelot.
find out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

first light.meaning: The time early in the morning when the sky first becomes light.
first light.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

for a moment.example: The magician was silent for a moment.
for a moment.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

for now.meaning: For a short time; until later. "Good-bye for now" means good-bye until we meet again.
for now.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

for sale.example: Kids were waving souvenir programs, soccer shirts, and caps for sale.
for sale.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

for sure.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

free kick.meaning: In soccer, a kick that a team gets when the other team breaks a rule. No one can stop the kicker.
free kick.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

game of a lifetime.meaning: The best game you will ever see in your whole life.
game of a lifetime.example: “It’s going to be the game of a lifetime!”
game of a lifetime.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get a good look.meaning: To see something well and clearly.
get a good look.example: Not only would he never get a good look at the World Cup players now—but how was he going to find Annie again?
get a good look.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get around.meaning: To travel from place to place ("get around the city").
get around.example: He was also amazed that a ten-year-old could get around the city so easily.
get around.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get back.example: She turned to Roberto and asked, “Roberto, can you help us get back into the city?”
get back.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get close to.example: But before they could even get close to the train, a bell rang and the doors slammed shut.
get close to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get it.meaning: (Friendly talk.) To understand. "I get it" means "I understand."
get it.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get lost.meaning: To not know where you are or how to get back.
get lost.example: “Just ask somebody if you get lost,” said Benny.
get lost.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

get off.meaning: To leave a boat, bus or train.
get off.example: Then we get off at the last stop and get a tram to Aztec Stadium!”
get off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get out of here.meaning: "Let's get out of here!" means "Let's leave this place now!"
get out of here.example: “Let’s get out of here,” said Jack.
get out of here.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get ready.meaning: To make yourself ready for something.
get ready.example: As the train slowed for the next stop, Jack and Annie both got ready to jump out of their seats.
get ready.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

get to.meaning: 1. To reach a place. 2. "The warnings had gotten to him" = they began to worry him.
get to.example: He knew he had to get to the top.
get to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

give something a try.meaning: To try to do something, to see if it works.
give something a try.example: Want to give it a try?”
give something a try.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

give up.example: “Even though Italy was behind, they never gave up,” said Roberto.
give up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

go back.example: And then we go back to Camelot to meet up with Merlin!”
go back.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

go wild.meaning: (of a crowd) To become very excited and noisy.
go wild.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

gobble up.meaning: To eat something quickly and greedily.
gobble up.example: Jack gobbled up tacos filled with tomatoes, chilies, and cheese.
gobble up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

good luck.meaning: I hope things go well for you.
good luck.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

grab a bite.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

grow up.meaning: To become an adult; to be a child who is getting older.
grow up.example: His dad had told them that kids rarely played soccer when he was growing up.
grow up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

had better.meaning: "We'd better go" means we should go, or something bad may happen.
had better.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

hold on to.example: There were no empty seats, so they stood in the aisle and held on to a pole.
hold on to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

hold out.meaning: To move your hand forward with something in it, to show it or give it.
hold out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

hold up.meaning: To lift something and hold it high, so people can see it.
hold up.example: She held up two purple tickets.
hold up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

i'm afraid.meaning: "I'm afraid ..." is a polite way to say something sad or bad: "I am sorry to say ..."
i'm afraid.example: “But I’m afraid your seat is in a different section,” said the usher.
i'm afraid.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in big trouble.meaning: In a very bad or dangerous situation.
in big trouble.example: On their last two missions, they’d found themselves in big trouble when their magic hour of greatness had ended.
in big trouble.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in fact.meaning: Really; the truth is. People say "in fact" to add something more surprising.
in fact.example: “Don’t worry,” said Annie. “It’ll become more popular with time. In fact, by 2014—”
in fact.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in front of.example: We landed in front of the U.
in front of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in particular.meaning: "To no one in particular" = not to one special person; to anyone who could hear.
in particular.example: Jack yelled to no one in particular.
in particular.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in the distance.meaning: Far away, but you can still see or hear it.
in the distance.example: She pointed to the huge statue of a winged angel looming in the distance.
in the distance.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in the middle of.meaning: In the centre of a place, or during an event.
in the middle of.example: “It looks like we landed in the middle of the city,” said Jack.
in the middle of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in the world.meaning: "The greatest in the world" = better than any other anywhere.
in the world.example: Mexico City is one of the largest cities in the world.
in the world.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

jump in.meaning: To start talking suddenly, often to stop a problem.
jump in.example: Before Roberto could answer, another boy jumped in.
jump in.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

jump to your feet.meaning: To stand up very quickly, often because you are excited.
jump to your feet.example: Then thousands of Brazil fans jumped to their feet, pumping their fists in the air and screaming, “Gooooaaaallll!!!!”
jump to your feet.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

just as.meaning: 1. At the same moment that. 2. In the same way that.
just as.example: “Yes, but it will be just as crowded,” Roberto answered.
just as.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

just in time.meaning: Not too late; at the last moment.
just in time.example: Out of breath, they got to the bus stop just in time.
just in time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

keep your eye on.example: Just make sure to keep your eye on it when we’re with Pelé.”
keep your eye on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

kind of.meaning: 1. A little; quite. (Friendly talk.) 2. "All kinds of" = many different types of ("all kinds of fish").
kind of.example: “Our lives are kind of crazy,” said Annie.
kind of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

knock over.meaning: To hit someone or something so that they fall down.
knock over.example: As he looked around, he was accidentally knocked over by rowdy teenagers dancing in the aisle, screaming and waving flags.
knock over.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

known as.meaning: Called by a name. "Better known as Pelé" = most people call him Pelé.
known as.example: They are the daughter and grandson of one of the greatest soccer players of all time—the Brazilian player Edson Arantes do Nascimento, better known as Pelé.
known as.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

let out.meaning: To make a sound, or to breathe out. "Let out a sigh" means sighed. "Let out a breath" means breathed out.
let out.example: Suddenly all the spectators let out a roar.
let out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

let up.meaning: (Of rain) to stop or become less strong.
let up.example: The rain had let up and there was a steamy mist in the air.
let up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

look around.meaning: To look at the things or places around you, often to find something.
look around.example: She and Jack looked around the tree house for a book that would help them on their journey.
look around.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

look for.example: “Oh, we were just looking for information,” said Jack.
look for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

look like.meaning: To seem to be something, because of how it looks.
look like.example: “It looks like we landed in the middle of the city,” said Jack.
look like.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

look up.meaning: 1. To raise your eyes and look up ("Jack looked up"). 2. To look for a fact in a book ("I'd better look this up").
look up.example: When Jack and Annie came to the tallest oak in the woods, they looked up into the branches.
